title: Populism
hook: Populism isn't a single program — it's a style that splits society into two camps: a virtuous 'people' against a corrupt 'elite,' with the populist speaking for the people.
key_points: Populism frames politics as a struggle between 'the pure people' and a 'corrupt elite.'
It is a style or thin ideology that attaches to left-wing, right-wing, or other agendas.
It claims to embody the people's true will, often distrusting mediating institutions.
It can energize neglected voters but may strain checks, minority rights, and pluralism.
content_html: Populism is one of the most-used and most-slippery words in modern politics. It is best understood not as a fixed program but as a way of framing politics: a division of society into two antagonistic camps — "the pure people" on one side and "the corrupt elite" on the other — with the populist claiming to be the authentic voice of the people against that elite. Because this frame says little about what policies the people should get, scholars often call populism a "thin" ideology or a political style that attaches itself to a fuller agenda.
extra_html: That is why populism appears across the spectrum: there are left-wing populists who target economic elites and right-wing populists who target cultural or political establishments, drawing on very different substantive ideologies while sharing the same people-versus-elite structure. Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that populists typically claim to embody the people's single, true will, which leads to a characteristic distrust of mediating institutions — courts, the press, expert bodies, even opposition parties — that stand between the leader and "the people." This has two faces. Populism can energize voters who feel ignored and force neglected grievances onto the agenda, acting as a corrective to a complacent establishment. But the claim to be the sole legitimate voice of the people can also strain the parts of democracy designed to protect pluralism and minorities — independent checks, the rights of those who disagree, and the acceptance that no single group speaks for everyone.

flashcards.prompt: What basic division does populism draw?
flashcards.back_html: Between "the pure people" and "a corrupt elite," with the populist claiming to speak for the people against the elite.

flashcards.prompt: Why is populism described as a 'thin' ideology or a style?

choices.text: It attaches to left-wing, right-wing, or other agendas rather than being a full program
Because it only ever appears in small countries
Because it has no view of who 'the people' are

flashcards.explanation_html: Populism supplies a people-versus-elite frame but borrows its substantive goals from whatever fuller ideology it attaches to.

flashcards.prompt: What is a commonly cited risk of populism in a democracy?

choices.text: Claiming sole voice of 'the people' can strain checks, minority rights, and pluralism

flashcards.explanation_html: If one leader or movement claims to embody the people's single true will, it can treat opposition and institutional limits as illegitimate.
